extracted.intended_audience: educated readers or students of philosophy / moral psychology (early-modern audience)
extracted.subtask_description: A philosophical treatise excerpt outlining standards for clear reasoning, the nature and classification of human passions, signs of science and prudence, and intellectual virtues; meant to guide understanding and evaluation of discourse, action, and character. It provides definitions, distinctions, and anti-patterns for speech, inquiry, and moral-psychological diagnosis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid metaphoric or ambiguous speech in pursuit of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: In reckoning and seeking truth, speeches that attribute actions to inanimate things (e.g., 'The Way Goeth', 'The Proverb Sayes') or use loose metaphor are not to be admitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphors and senseless or ambiguous words are like ignes fatui; reasoning upon them leads to innumerable absurdities, contention, sedition, or contempt. Ordinary colloquial metaphor may be tolerated in common speech but must be purged for precise enquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid names that signify nothing (scholastic cant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject learned rote terms that have no clear meaning (examples: 'Hypostatical', 'Transubstantiate', 'Consubstantiate', 'Eternal-now').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such canting school-words lead to confusion; prefer exact definitions and perspicuous words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Science
rubrics_metrics.description: Science consists of apt imposing of names and an orderly method proceeding from elements (names) to assertions and syllogisms, giving knowledge of consequences and dependencies among facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science differs from sense and memory (knowledge of fact) by enabling one, from knowledge of causes and manner, to reproduce effects when similar causes are in one's power. Science is attained by industry (method and naming).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason is attained by industry, not innate
rubrics_metrics.description: Reason is not innate like sense or memory; it is acquired by imposing names and learning orderly methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Children are not endowed with reason until speech; training in beginnings and progress of sciences is necessary to produce sapience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: Prudence (experience) vs Sapience (science)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prudence arises from experience; sapience from much science. Prudence guides practical life, sapience produces infallible ability when present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying on books or false rules (trusting the blind) can lead to worse outcomes than natural prudence. Sapience (science-backed knowledge) is superior when genuinely established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of Science vs Signs of Prudence
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain sign of a professed science is the ability to teach/demonstrate it perspicuously; uncertain signs are when only some events match the claim. Signs of prudence are necessarily uncertain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forsaking one's natural judgement to be guided by general sentences from authors (pedantry) is a sign of folly. In public counsel many display reading rather than genuine practical prudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two kinds of animal motion: vital and voluntary
rubrics_metrics.description: Vitall motions (blood, pulse, breathing, nutrition) proceed without imagination; animal (voluntary) motions (going, speaking, moving limbs) are preceded by imagination/endeavour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voluntary motion always depends on a prior thought (whither, which way, what); the small internal beginnings before visible action are called endeavour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appetite/Desire and Aversion defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Endeavour toward something is Appetite or Desire (Appetite often for food); endeavour from something is Aversion. Love/Hate correspond to presence/absence distinctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Desire and Love differ: Desire implies absence of object, Love implies presence; Aversion vs Hate similarly. Some appetites are innate (food, excretion), others arise from experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contempt identified as immobility or contumacy of the heart
rubrics_metrics.description: Contempt is the state of neither desiring nor hating, an immobility or stubborn resistance of the heart often due to being moved by more potent objects or lack of experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because bodily constitution changes, same objects will not always cause identical appetites or aversions across time or persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good and Evil are relative to the person or authority
rubrics_metrics.description: What a man desires he calls Good; what he hates he calls Evil. There is nothing simply or absolutely good or evil — the standard is the person, the commonwealth, or an arbitrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral predicates are relative; in a commonwealth, the person who represents it or an arbitrator's sentence makes the rule of good/evil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three kinds of 'Good' (pulchrum, jucundum, utile) and corresponding evils
rubrics_metrics.description: Good in promise (pulchrum), Good in effect/end (jucundum, delightfull), Good as means (utile, profitable). Evils mirror these: turpe (in promise), molestum (in effect), inutile (in means).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate vocabulary to distinguish promise, effect, and means when evaluating value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure and Displeasure as appearances of appetites/aversions
rubrics_metrics.description: The real internal motion is endeavour (appetite/aversion); the apparent sense of that motion is Delight/Pleasure or Trouble/Displeasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleasure often corroborates vital motion and helps it; displeasure hinders vital motion—this links physiological utility to affective language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasures of Sense vs Pleasures of the Mind (joy) — and pains
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures from present sensation (sight, hearing, taste, etc.) are pleasures of sense. Pleasures from expectation of ends are pleasures of the mind (joy). Displeasures of sense are pain; displeasures of expectation are grief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate sensory pleasures from intellectual/anticipatory pleasures when describing affective states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hope
rubrics_metrics.description: Appetite with an opinion of attaining is called Hope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hope is distinguished from desire by the presence of an opinion about attainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Despair
rubrics_metrics.description: The same appetite without an opinion of attaining is Despair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of belief in attainment turns hopeful appetite into despair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Aversion combined with an opinion of hurt from the object is Fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fear is future-oriented aversion with expectation of harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage
rubrics_metrics.description: Aversion with hope of avoiding hurt by resistance is Courage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courage contains both apprehension and the belief in possibility of successful resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anger
rubrics_metrics.description: Sudden courage is Anger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anger is quick, energised courage often reactive in nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Constant hope is Confidence of ourselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steady expectation of success or capability underlies confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diffidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Constant despair is Diffidence of ourselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persistent lack of expectation of success defines diffidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indignation
rubrics_metrics.description: Anger for great hurt done to another, conceived as injury to them, is Indignation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indignation presupposes concern for another and moral evaluation of injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benevolence (Good Will)
rubrics_metrics.description: Desire of good to another is Benevolence, Good Will, or Charity; if general to all men, called Good Nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benevolence is other-directed desire for good; scope distinguishes benevolence from general good nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covetousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Desire of riches is Covetousness; term usually blameworthy because contention over riches displeases others, though desire itself may be approved depending on means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate covetousness partly by the means and social consequences of the pursuit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambition
rubrics_metrics.description: Desire of office or precedence is Ambition; often used pejoratively for similar reasons as covetousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambition's moral valence depends on context and means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pusillanimity
rubrics_metrics.description: Desire of things that conduce little to our ends and fear of trivial hindrances is Pusillanimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small-mindedness and excessive fear mark this defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnanimity
rubrics_metrics.description: Contempt of little helps and hindrances is Magnanimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large-mindedness; contrasted with pusillanimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valour / Fortitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Magnanimity in danger of death or wounds is Valour (Fortitude).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courage in the face of mortal danger qualifies as valour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberality
rubrics_metrics.description: Magnanimity in the use of riches is Liberality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generosity in distributing wealth reflects this virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miserableness / Parsimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Pusillanimity in the use of riches; parsimonious or wretched handling of wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Viewed negatively; relative to liberality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kindness
rubrics_metrics.description: Love of persons for society is Kindness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social affiliation and benevolence define kindness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural Lust
rubrics_metrics.description: Love of persons for pleasing the sense only is Natural Lust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguished from affectionate or social love by being sensual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Luxury
rubrics_metrics.description: Love acquired from rumination (imagination of past pleasure) is Luxury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imaginative indulgence in recalled pleasures fuels luxury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passion of Love; Jealousy
rubrics_metrics.description: Love of one singularly with desire to be singularly beloved is the Passion of Love; coupled with fear that love is not mutual, it becomes Jealousy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jealousy mixes desire and fear regarding mutuality of affection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revengefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Desire to do hurt to another to make him condemn some fact of his own is Revengefulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revenge is other-directed vindictive desire; morally suspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curiosity
rubrics_metrics.description: Desire to know why and how; a passion proper to man, distinguishing him from other animals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curiosity is the intellectual lust that drives knowledge-seeking beyond mere sensory aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion vs Superstition; True Religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear of invisible power imagined by the mind or from tales is Religion (if wrongly imagined, called superstition). When the imagined power is truly such, it is True Religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish fear based on imagination/tale (superstition) from fear grounded in true relation to power (true religion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Panique Terror
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear without apprehension of why or what (panic terror) occurs typically in crowds where each supposes another knows the cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panique terror arises in throngs by contagion; there is often at least some initial apprehension though the rest follow by example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admiration
rubrics_metrics.description: Joy from apprehension of novelty is Admiration; it excites the appetite of knowing the cause and is proper to man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admiration stimulates curiosity and knowledge-seeking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glory and Vaine-glory
rubrics_metrics.description: Joy arising from imagination of one's own power and ability is Glorying; if grounded on experience, equals Confidence; if grounded on flattery or self-supposition, it is Vaine-glory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vaine-glory produces delight without effective attempt; confidence leads to action. Vaine-glory is common in youth and corrected by age and employment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Grief from opinion of want of power is Dejection of mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loss of perceived capacity causes dejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sudden Glory (Laughter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sudden glory causes Laughter; produced by a sudden act of one's own pleasing them or by apprehension of deformity in another by comparison, producing self-applause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive laughter at others' defects is a sign of pusillanimity; great minds aim to help and free others from scorn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sudden Dejection (Weeping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sudden dejection causes Weeping; produced by sudden loss of vehement hope or prop of power. Custome reduces both laughter and weeping for old matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weeping often follows sudden thwarting of hope; those dependent on external helps (women, children) more subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shame (Blushing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Grief for discovery of some defect of ability is Shame, manifesting as Blushing; in young men it indicates love of reputation and is commendable, in old men less so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shame signals concern for honour; contempt of good reputation is Impudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pity (Compassion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Grief for the calamity of another arising from imagining the same calamity may befall oneself; called Pitty, Compassion, or Fellow-feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those least feeling pity for given calamities are those who think themselves least exposed to them; the best men have least pity for calamity arising from great wickedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cruelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Contempt or little sense of the calamity of others, proceeding from security of one's own fortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author doubts that anyone could take pleasure in others' great harms without some end of their own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emulation vs Envy
rubrics_metrics.description: Grief for a competitor's success joined with endeavour to equal or exceed is Emulation; joined with endeavour to supplant or hinder is Envy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emulation can be constructive, envy destructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberation
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole sum of alternate Appetites, Aversions, Hopes and Fears concerning the same thing, continued until the thing is done or thought impossible, is Deliberation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberation does not occur about past unchangeable facts or things known impossible. It ends when action is taken or the matter is judged impossible. Beasts also deliberate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Will (act of willing)
rubrics_metrics.description: In deliberation, the last appetite or aversion immediately adhering to the action or omission is called the Will (the act, not the faculty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A voluntary act proceeds from the will (the final inclination). Earlier inclinations that do not adhere to the final appetite are mere inclinations and do not make an act voluntary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of speech expressing passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Passions can be expressed in different grammatical moods: Indicative (I love, I fear), Subjunctive for Deliberation (If this be done...), Imperative for desire/aversion (Do this), Optative for vaine-glory/indignation/pity/revenge, Interrogative for desire to know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are voluntary significations and not certain proofs of the passions; better signs are countenance, bodily motions, actions, and aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparent Good and Evil in Deliberation
rubrics_metrics.description: In deliberation, appetites and aversions arise from foresight of a chain of consequences; the balance (apparent good or seeming good vs apparent evill) depends on how far one can see consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those with the largest and surest prospect of consequences deliberate best and can give best counsel; foresight is the key to good deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Felicity (happiness) defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Continual success in obtaining those things a man desires (continual prospering) is called Felicity of this life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no perpetual tranquillity while living; life is motion and cannot be without desire or fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Praise and Magnification as forms of appraisal
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise expresses opinion of goodness; magnifying expresses opinion of power/greatness; Greek 'makarismos' denotes opinion of a man's felicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise the rhetorical forms that convey evaluative judgements in discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgement, Opinion, Conscience, Faith distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusion of a syllogistic discourse is Science; when discourse doesn't start at definitions, its end is Opinion. Conscience denotes common knowledge among witnesses; Faith/Belief arise when one accepts a saying from authority rather than from principles or reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful to distinguish knowledge derived from demonstration (science), from opinion based on authority, and from conscience-based mutual knowledge; the phrase 'I believe in' in ecclesiastical use denotes confession rather than trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual virtue defined and distinguished
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellectual virtues are abilities of mind praised for eminence; include natural or acquired wit, judgement, discretion, and fancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural wit (from use/experience without method) comprises celerity of imagining and steady direction; dulness is the lack thereof. Acquired virtues come from culture, method, and instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good Fancy vs Good Judgement vs Discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Good Fancy (wit) arises from observing rare similitudes and inventing rare metaphors; Good Judgement is discerning differences and practical discernment; Discretion is judgement about times, places, persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In poetry, fancy should be more eminent (for extravagance), tempered by discretion; in history, judgement and method are paramount. Excessive fancy without steadiness causes digressions and loss of purpose (a kind of madness).
